title: Pop radio, the Harley Show, teacher Sonny Costanza and Quinnipiac band
summary: Asked about pop music, he recalls late-night jazz radio from Baltimore, studying with Sonny Costanza and playing with the Quinnipiac College band and visiting stars.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What about — you and I are the same age actually I noticed—
You’re old enough to be my brother.
There you go. But I remember being turned on to pop music, like Little Eva and “The Locomotion” and that kind of stuff that was on AM radio. Did that stuff make an impression on you?

Some of the pop stuff I discovered later It wasn’t like I was against it, and I can’t remember what instrument — and of course the Beatles were all around. I didn’t get the Beatles as much as I did later. But I don’t know, that’s a good question, because I can’t quite remember what really turned me on back then. I mean we listened to as much jazz as we could. But wide open. Like for instance, we lived in Fairfield, Connecticut, that’s where I lived, who’s we, I don’t — and there was a radio station in Baltimore — I can hardly remember the name now, but they had “The Harley Show,” this guy that made the Harley Sandwich Shop, he made these big subs and stuff. And he had this great jazz show. And in the summer, the AM signal skips. So you’d get it from a pretty far distance like that. And I used to get upstairs like at one in the morning with my little transistor radio. It was “The Harley Show” man. And “Things Ain’t What They Used to Be”, I can’t remember. But I started hearing a lot of Duke, I started — I’ll tell you the truth though, I was in jazz mostly. Later on I’ll probably remember some other rock stuff. I loved rock even at the beginning. I was never like, ooh, rock. And originally I loved Stan Kenton, and I said, “Aww this is great.” And I had a great teacher in New Haven, Connecticut named Sonny Costanza who used to play in Clark Terry’s big band. And he was a great teacher. He was more like a great trombonist who you sat next to him and you like, you learned a lot because he was just amazing. And he pushed me straight. And there was a college band out of Quinnipiac College, the Quinnipiac College Band it was called, it was like about 45 minutes from where I lived. So I used to go there. When I was being punished or stuff, and didn’t have the car, my mother would drive me. And so we would play, like Clark Terry was a guest once, a lot of those, oh yeah, Si Zentner, who, yeah, that’s right, and Kai Winding, I met all these guys.
Quinnipiac had a festival every year.
